heroLead: West Milford has spent the last decade and a half inside one of West Virginia's busiest drilling counties, and that changes what a mineral interest here is actually worth compared to quieter parts of the state.
intro: Harrison County has been a working center of Marcellus and Utica development for years, with multi-well pads, gathering lines, and compressor stations built out across the county as operators drilled longer laterals into both formations. West Milford sits inside that footprint, which means a mineral interest here isn't a legacy question the way it is in some quieter counties — it's often an active or recently active asset.

Before we make an offer on a West Milford tract, we pull the Harrison County record to confirm the mineral chain, check whether the interest is currently held under lease, and see whether it's included in a producing spacing unit or one that's been permitted but not yet drilled.

sections.heading: Harrison County's Modern Lateral Development
paragraphs: Operators active in Harrison County over the past fifteen years have consolidated older leaseholds into large horizontal spacing units, often pooling many small tracts into a single unit to support laterals that run a mile or more. If your West Milford interest was included in one of those units, it may already be generating royalty income, or it may be sitting in a unit that's permitted but not yet producing.
We check unit status directly rather than relying on what a landowner remembers being told when the lease was first signed, because that status changes the value of the interest substantially.

sections.heading: West Milford's Position on the Marcellus/Utica Play
paragraphs: West Milford sits well within Harrison County's productive core, not on its flank, which is part of why interests here tend to draw stronger offers than comparable tracts in counties further from the fairway. That doesn't mean every tract is equal — depth, thickness, and existing unit participation all vary parcel to parcel.
We look at the specific geology under your tract rather than the county it sits in alone before quoting a number.

sections.heading: Pooling, Spacing Units, and Flat-Rate Conversion
paragraphs: Some older leases on West Milford tracts predate the horizontal boom and were written as flat-rate agreements, which West Virginia law generally requires to convert to at least a 1/8 royalty once relevant production begins. If your tract got pulled into a modern spacing unit under an old flat-rate lease, that conversion should have happened, and we check whether it actually did before valuing the interest.
This is one of the most common gaps we find in Harrison County files — an old lease that never got formally updated even after new wells started producing under it.

sections.heading: Heirship on Century-Old Harrison County Tracts
paragraphs: Family farms around West Milford were frequently split among children generations ago, and those undivided shares have kept dividing further with each generation since. It's common to find six, ten, or more heirs holding fractional interests in a single tract, several of whom have never received a royalty check because the operator doesn't have current contact information for them.
We locate those interests through the Harrison County record and buy directly from individual heirs, without requiring the whole family to act together.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my West Milford tract is part of an active spacing unit?
faqs.answer: We check the Harrison County record and, where relevant, permit and unit filings to confirm whether your tract has been pooled into a producing or permitted unit before we make an offer.

faqs.question: I get a royalty check but it seems small for how much drilling has happened nearby. Why?
faqs.answer: Royalty amounts depend on your specific fractional interest, the size of the spacing unit, decline over time, and lease terms. We can review your division order and lease alongside the county record to see whether that's consistent with what's on file.

faqs.question: My family's old lease is flat-rate. Does that still apply if a new well was drilled nearby?
faqs.answer: It shouldn't, if the well produces under a spacing unit covering your tract — West Virginia's statutory floor generally requires conversion to at least a 1/8 royalty in that situation. We verify this before valuing your interest.

faqs.question: Do you buy fractional interests from just one heir in a larger family group?
faqs.answer: Yes, that's a normal transaction for us and doesn't require the rest of the family to participate or agree.
